name: Urban Mobility Study
description: A small made-up study of how people get around a city: three interviews, a focus group, a survey comment, and two other documents, with a codebook, codings, two cases, a memo, and a rating. Every word is invented for practice.
research_question: How do residents experience everyday public transit, and what would improve it?

documents.name: INT-001 – Alex
documents.text:
Interviewer: To start, can you tell me a bit about your daily travel routine?
Alex: Sure. I usually commute to work in the city center, so I travel about 12 kilometers each way.
Most days I take the bus because it's the most convenient option for me. The stops are close to my home, and I don't have to worry about parking, which would be a real hassle and expense downtown.
Interviewer: How would you describe your overall experience with public transportation?
Alex: It's generally okay, but reliability can be a problem. The bus is often late, especially in the mornings, and that can be stressful when I have a meeting. I've missed a few important things because of delays.
Interviewer: That sounds frustrating. Are there any other challenges you've noticed?
Alex: Cost is also a factor. The monthly pass is not cheap, and it adds up, especially with other living expenses. I think it's still better than owning a car, but it's something I have to budget for.
Interviewer: And looking ahead, what would make your travel experience better?
Alex: More frequent and reliable service would make a big difference. I'd also like to see more investment in sustainable options, like electric buses or better infrastructure for cycling. I think the city is moving in the right direction, but there's still a lot of room for improvement.
Interviewer: Is there anything else you'd like to add about urban mobility?
Alex: Just that it really affects quality of life. When it works well, it makes the city feel more accessible and livable. When it doesn't, it can be a daily source of stress. So it's an important area for the city to keep focusing on.

documents.name: INT-002 – Priya
documents.text:
Interviewer: How do you get to work?
Priya: I take the train most days. The trains are usually good, but when there's a signal failure everything stops and I have no backup plan.
Interviewer: What would help?
Priya: Clear announcements, and a bus that runs when the line is down.

documents.name: INT-003 – Jordan
documents.text:
Interviewer: What do you use most?
Jordan: I switch between the bus and cycling depending on the weather and how early I need to be at the office.
Interviewer: Is there anything that stops you from cycling more?
Jordan: Safe lanes. There are stretches where I do not feel safe at all.

documents.name: FG-001 – Commuters
documents.text:
Moderator: What changed after the new line opened?
Participant A: Mostly the evenings felt safer, and the platforms are easier to reach.
Participant B: For me it is the cost. The fares went up in the same month.

documents.name: SR-001 – Survey comments
documents.text:
Respondent 14: Bike lanes would make me ride more.
Respondent 22: I would use the bus if it came more often.

documents.name: LIT-001 – Transit equity
documents.text: Access to frequent service is unevenly spread across neighborhoods, and the cost of a monthly pass weighs more on lower incomes.

documents.name: MED-001 – Council recording notes
documents.text: Council meeting notes on the proposed bus priority lanes: speakers asked for safer crossings and for a trial of electric buses on two routes.
